paragraphs: Thompson Sampling makes sequential decisions by sampling from estimates of how rewarding each available option might be. Strong average performance can still coexist with unfavorable outcomes in some runs or sensitivity to incorrect modeling assumptions. This paper studies how changing the sampling variance can improve those aspects of Gaussian Thompson Sampling.

The proposed modification introduces a variance inflation factor that depends on both time and the particular option being considered. The authors establish worst-case optimal expected regret and worst-case optimal bounds on how quickly the probability of large regret decreases. Their results also cover sub-exponential noise and misspecified environments, and the policy tolerates incorrectly specified noise variances.

The analysis extends beyond rewards accumulated during the experiment. It also gives rapidly decreasing tail probabilities for simple regret and estimation error for each option, supporting more reliable decisions afterward. An extension handles unknown variances that differ across options. Experiments report consistent performance across multiple environments, complementing the theoretical account of how this small policy change improves reliability.
neurips-2025-adaptive-variance-inflation.tldr: A time- and option-dependent increase in Thompson Sampling variance improves regret guarantees, robustness, and the reliability of decisions made after experimentation.

paragraphs: Reasoning models can spend many tokens working through tasks that do not require lengthy deliberation. ARM addresses this inefficiency by learning to select a reasoning format appropriate to the task. Its choices are a direct answer, a short chain of thought, code, or a longer chain of thought.

Training uses Ada-GRPO, a modification of Group Relative Policy Optimization designed to address format collapse. Maintaining multiple usable formats matters because adaptive reasoning depends on choosing among them. The authors report about 30% fewer tokens on average and reductions reaching about 70%, while retaining performance comparable to a model that always uses long reasoning. They also report roughly twice the training speed.

ARM provides three ways to manage this flexibility. Its default mode selects formats automatically, while an instruction-guided mode lets users request one explicitly. A consensus-guided mode combines the three efficient formats and invokes long reasoning when they disagree. That last mode prioritizes performance at greater token cost, making the efficiency tradeoff an explicit part of the system.
neurips-2025-arm-adaptive-reasoning-mode.tldr: ARM learns to choose among four reasoning formats, reducing token use while preserving performance comparable to always using lengthy reasoning.

paragraphs: Training one reinforcement learning agent across many tasks is difficult when rewards are sparse and updates from different tasks conflict. These problems make temporal-difference learning brittle. The paper examines whether larger value models can support effective online multi-task learning, extending a scaling approach that has worked well in language and vision.

The proposed approach combines high-capacity value functions, cross-entropy training, and learnable task embeddings. The embeddings condition the model on the task, allowing a shared value model to distinguish the objectives it is learning. The authors report that this combination addresses interference between tasks and enables robust, scalable training through online interaction.

Evaluation covers seven multi-task benchmarks containing more than 280 distinct tasks, including complex humanoid control and discrete tasks driven by visual observations. The authors report state-of-the-art performance in both single-task and multi-task settings, alongside sample-efficient transfer to new tasks. These findings support the usefulness of a shared, high-capacity value model for learning diverse behaviors, including workflows that learn online instead of depending on expert cloning or policy distillation.
neurips-2025-bigger-regularized-categori.tldr: Large value models trained with cross-entropy and task embeddings reduce task interference and deliver strong online multi-task reinforcement learning performance.

paragraphs: Counterfactual explanations recommend changes that help an individual obtain a desired outcome at low personal cost. But recommendations interact when many people pursue similar changes. Competition can create additional costs, and advice that ignores the surrounding data distribution can appear unusual or impractical. This paper brings those population effects into the recommendation problem.

The framework incorporates a model of population dynamics and penalizes departures from equilibrium after people act on the advice. It therefore balances the cost of each person's changes against consequences for others. Recommendations become a collective optimization problem, with their quality assessed partly through the population state they produce.

The authors contribute theoretical insights and scalable algorithms for computing these collective counterfactuals. They demonstrate advantages over existing recourse methods, particularly in alignment with collective objectives. The significance is that individually inexpensive advice can have shared costs when adopted together. Accounting for those interactions gives the framework a way to mitigate externalities and pursue more equitable and efficient outcomes across the population.
neurips-2025-collective-counterfactual-e.tldr: Collective counterfactual explanations account for population dynamics so that individually useful recommendations also consider their effects on others.

paragraphs: Generating video frames between widely spaced keyframes becomes especially difficult when people perform complex movements. Existing methods draw on pretrained video diffusion models, but without three-dimensional guidance they can struggle with articulated motion and offer limited control. PoseFuse3D-KI adds information about human geometry to guide the intermediate frames.

Its control model, PoseFuse3D, includes an SMPL-X encoder that represents three-dimensional geometry and body shape in the two-dimensional latent space used for conditioning. A fusion network then combines those signals with two-dimensional pose embeddings. This connects structural information about the person with the generative model's process for producing video, giving interpolation richer spatial cues.

The authors also introduce CHKI-Video, an evaluation dataset containing both two-dimensional pose annotations and three-dimensional SMPL-X parameters. On this dataset, PoseFuse3D-KI consistently outperforms the compared state-of-the-art methods, with a reported 9% improvement in PSNR and 38% reduction in LPIPS. Ablation experiments further support the contribution of PoseFuse3D to interpolation fidelity. Together, the results show the value of incorporating explicit human geometry into this controlled interpolation setting.
neurips-2025-controllable-human-centric-.tldr: PoseFuse3D-KI uses three-dimensional human geometry to improve control and fidelity when generating video frames between keyframes.

paragraphs: Text-guided image editing often starts by reconstructing the generative path that could have produced a source image. Errors in this inversion can then limit the edit. The paper identifies a difficulty with diffusion-based inversion: intermediate generative steps lack exact supervision, so the recovered trajectory can contain approximation errors.

EditInfinity adapts Infinity, a binary-quantized generative model, using a parameter-efficient approach. Quantized models make exact intermediate representations of a source image available, supplying supervision for more precise inversion. The proposed inversion mechanism combines text prompting rectification with preservation of image style. A further smoothing strategy helps editing retain source-image fidelity while matching the requested text.

The authors evaluate the system on PIE-Bench across operations that add, change, and delete image content. They report superior performance over state-of-the-art diffusion-based baselines. The contribution connects the choice of generative representation to editing accuracy: accessible intermediate representations help reconstruct the source, while the editing strategy balances requested semantic changes with preservation of the original image.
neurips-2025-editinfinity-image-editing-.tldr: EditInfinity uses exact intermediate quantized representations to improve image inversion and produce faithful text-guided edits.

paragraphs: A deep reinforcement learning network can organize inputs by their meaning within its internal feature space. This paper studies that organization as a route to interpretability. The central question is whether groups of semantically similar inputs can reveal useful structure in what a policy has learned and how it represents its experiences.

The authors introduce an architecture with a semantic clustering module that combines dimensionality reduction with online clustering. Dimensionality reduction makes the feature representation more compact, while clustering identifies related inputs during training. The module fits into the reinforcement learning pipeline, addresses the instability associated with t-SNE, and avoids the extensive manual annotation required by earlier semantic analysis methods.

Experiments demonstrate that the module exposes semantic clustering within deep reinforcement learning networks. The paper also develops analytical methods that use these clusters to examine policy hierarchy and the organization of feature space. The stated benefit is a clearer view of internal semantic structure, providing a basis for studying how learned policies organize related situations.
neurips-2025-enhancing-interpretability-.tldr: An online semantic clustering module reveals how deep reinforcement learning networks organize related inputs and structure their policies.

paragraphs: In mixed-motive games, agents have reasons to cooperate but also pursue their own rewards. Improving the group's total return does not by itself resolve whether individual agents benefit fairly. This paper addresses both concerns within multi-agent reinforcement learning, focusing on fairness in the rewards associated with each agent's task.

The method adjusts policy gradients when the individual and collective objectives conflict. These gradients indicate how learning would change behavior to improve the respective objectives. Dynamically balancing them lets the method respond directly to conflicting learning directions. This places fairness and cooperation within the policy update process, beyond the tradeoffs managed by reward restructuring methods such as gifting or intrinsic motivation.

The authors provide theoretical results guaranteeing non-decreasing improvement in both individual and collective objectives, together with fairness. Experiments in sequential social dilemma environments report higher social welfare than the compared baselines while maintaining fairness. The theoretical and empirical contributions jointly support the approach's aim: improving cooperation while preserving attention to the rewards of the individual agents involved.
neurips-2025-fair-cooperation-in-mixed-m.tldr: Conflict-aware policy gradient adjustments promote cooperation while supporting fairness and non-decreasing individual and collective objectives.

paragraphs: Local search improves clustering by replacing selected cluster centers, but repeatedly scanning the full dataset makes these swaps expensive. This paper accelerates two parts of that process: sampling promising candidates and choosing which swap to make. It aims to preserve approximation guarantees while reducing the cost of working with large datasets.

Adaptive sampling approximates the desired distance-based distribution without maintaining distances between every point and the centers. After preprocessing with a near-linear dependence on data size and dimension, sampling takes sublinear time. A bandit formulation then treats swap selection as a search among alternatives, using grouping to identify the best pair efficiently.

Under mild assumptions on optimal clusters and swap-pair distributions, the algorithm achieves a constant approximation in expected time approximately nd + k⁴, suppressing logarithmic factors. Its k-median extension achieves a corresponding bound of approximately nd + √n k³ without distributional assumptions. Experiments report up to 1,000-fold speedups over existing local search on 100-million-point datasets with comparable quality, and up to 80-fold speedups over coreset approaches with consistently better clustering results.
neurips-2025-fast-local-search-algorithm.tldr: Adaptive sampling and bandit-based swap selection accelerate clustering local search while retaining constant-approximation guarantees under the stated conditions.

paragraphs: Federated learning must handle more than a fixed collection of clients when new participants continually arrive. Incoming clients can introduce unfamiliar data domains or additional classes. Gains addresses the paired challenges of recognizing this new knowledge and incorporating it into a global model without sacrificing performance for existing clients.

The approach separates the model into an encoder and a classifier. The authors empirically find that encoder features respond to domain shifts, while classifier parameters respond to increases in the number of classes. Gains uses these distinct signals for finer-grained knowledge discovery. A contribution-driven aggregation method incorporates the new knowledge, and an anti-forgetting mechanism helps preserve performance on source domains.

Experiments use multi-domain datasets across three data-shift scenarios. Gains significantly outperforms the compared baselines for both source-domain and target-domain clients. The results support treating discovery and adaptation as connected tasks: distinguishing the kind of change introduced by new clients helps guide integration, while explicit protection against forgetting helps balance benefits across old and new participants.
neurips-2025-gains-fine-grained-federate.tldr: Gains distinguishes domain shifts from new classes to integrate incoming federated clients' knowledge while preserving performance for existing clients.

paragraphs: This paper studies calibration for forecasts with multiple dimensions, allowing predictions in any convex set and measuring error with any norm. It connects the achievable calibration rate to online linear optimization: if that optimization problem admits worst-case regret O(√(ρT)), then ε-calibrated forecasting is possible after exp(O(ρ/ε²)) rounds.

The algorithm does not need an online linear optimization subroutine or prior knowledge of the best rate parameter ρ. Instead, the analysis uses an optimal regularizer to bound calibration error through swap regret. The method minimizes that regret with TreeSwap and Follow-The-Leader. Each round, it selects from a distribution over simple averages of previous observations, giving an efficient computational procedure.

For forecasts on a d-dimensional probability simplex with ℓ₁ error, the resulting round bound is d raised to O(1/ε²). The paper also proves that exponential dependence on inverse accuracy is necessary when the dimension is sufficiently large relative to inverse accuracy. Thus, efficient computation per round coexists with an unavoidable accuracy-related burden on the number of rounds.
neurips-2025-high-dimensional-calibratio.tldr: A swap-regret method connects multidimensional forecast calibration to online optimization rates and establishes an unavoidable exponential dependence on inverse accuracy.

paragraphs: LLaDA investigates whether capabilities associated with large language models can emerge from diffusion-based language modeling. The model is trained from scratch through pretraining and supervised fine-tuning. Its forward process masks text, and a Transformer learns the reverse process by predicting masked tokens. Training optimizes a lower bound on likelihood, providing a probabilistic basis for generation.

Across benchmarks involving general tasks, mathematics, and code, the authors report strong scaling behavior and performance comparable to their own autoregressive baselines. The eight-billion-parameter version is also competitive with LLaMA3 8B in in-context learning. After supervised fine-tuning, case studies show instruction-following abilities, including multi-turn dialogue.

The paper additionally examines the reversal curse and reports that LLaDA surpasses GPT-4o on a reversal poem completion task. That result concerns the specified task, while the broader evidence supports diffusion as a promising approach to language modeling at scale. Together, the findings challenge the idea that the demonstrated capabilities inherently require an autoregressive model.
neurips-2025-large-language-diffusion-mo.tldr: LLaDA shows that masked-token diffusion models can scale and develop several language-model capabilities commonly associated with autoregressive training.

paragraphs: Multi-agent assistants can be difficult to move between domains when their architecture and training are tightly tied to one setting. Workforce separates general planning from specialized execution. A Planner decomposes tasks, a Coordinator manages subtasks, and Workers provide the tool-calling capabilities needed for particular domains.

This modular structure supports transfer during inference by adding or modifying Workers. Optimized Workforce Learning, or OWL, addresses the training side: it uses reinforcement learning with real-world feedback to improve the domain-agnostic Planner. The aim is to make planning generalize across domains while allowing execution capabilities to remain specialized.

On GAIA, which covers realistic tasks across multiple domains, Workforce achieves 69.70% performance and is reported as the strongest open-source system in the comparison, exceeding OpenAI's Deep Research by 2.34%. The OWL-trained 32B model reaches 52.73% accuracy, with a reported improvement of 16.37%, and performs comparably to GPT-4o on challenging tasks. These results support the combination of modular execution and learned general planning for the evaluated automation tasks.
neurips-2025-owl-optimized-workforce-lea.tldr: Workforce separates planning from specialized workers, while OWL trains the general planner to improve cross-domain task automation.

paragraphs: Learning from unlabeled point clouds can reduce dependence on costly three-dimensional annotations. However, masked autoencoders often receive patch-center coordinates as positional information, exposing geometry that the model could otherwise learn to infer. Point-MaDi changes the pretraining task so that recovering spatial structure becomes part of the learning problem.

Its encoder adds noise to the centers of both visible and masked patches and predicts their coordinates without ground-truth positional embeddings. Self-attention and cross-attention process the predicted centers to capture relationships within and between patches. The decoder then reconstructs masked patches from noise, conditioned on the encoder's features and predicted centers. These two diffusion processes target global semantic structure and local geometry together.

Experiments across ScanObjectNN, ModelNet40, ShapeNetPart, S3DIS, and ScanNet report superior downstream performance. For ScanObjectNN classification, the reported gains over Point-MAE are 5.51% on OBJ-BG, 5.17% on OBJ-ONLY, and 4.34% on PB-T50-RS. The results support making center prediction and patch reconstruction complementary pretraining tasks, reducing reliance on externally supplied geometric priors.
neurips-2025-point-madi-masked-autoencod.tldr: Point-MaDi learns point-cloud structure by jointly denoising patch centers and reconstructing masked patches, improving downstream three-dimensional recognition.

paragraphs: Long-context language generation requires storing a large key-value cache. Compressing that cache with lower-precision numbers saves memory, but unusually large values make key states difficult to quantize accurately. PolarQuant addresses this problem by changing the representation of keys before quantization, using structure associated with rotary position embeddings.

The authors observe that outliers generally occur in one of two dimensions that rotary embeddings rotate together. Viewed as a two-dimensional vector, each pair has a radius and angle whose distributions are smoother in polar space. PolarQuant divides key vectors into such pairs and quantizes their radii and angles. This representation alleviates the channel-wise outliers that complicate direct quantization.

The method also replaces the query-key inner product computation with a table lookup to accelerate decoding. The authors report improved cache-quantization efficiency and faster decoding while maintaining the downstream performance of full-precision models. The contribution links memory compression with computation: representing keys in polar coordinates supports both lower-bit storage and a more efficient way to evaluate their interaction with queries.
neurips-2025-polarquant-leveraging-polar.tldr: PolarQuant encodes key-cache pairs as quantized radii and angles, reducing outlier problems and accelerating decoding through table lookups.

paragraphs: Safety fine-tuning can make a language model refuse harmless questions when training data repeatedly pairs unsafe prompts with standard refusal templates. This paper examines that overgeneralization through both the diversity of the training text and the geometry of internal representations. The authors measure substantially lower token entropy and two-word diversity in safety data than in general instruction data.

They introduce FlowLens, a stable analysis tool based on principal component analysis, to inspect the residual stream. Increasing the proportion of safety examples concentrates representational variance in fewer components and reduces smoothness. In the reported setting, false refusals rise from 63% to 84% as the safety-data proportion increases from zero to 40%.

These observations motivate Variance Concentration Loss, an auxiliary training penalty that discourages excessive concentration in middle-layer residual representations. Experiments show a reduction in false refusals of more than 35 percentage points while maintaining or improving results on general benchmarks, including MMLU and GSM8K. The findings connect a measurable internal representation pattern with a practical intervention against unnecessary refusals.
neurips-2025-residual-stream-analysis-of.tldr: FlowLens links repetitive safety training to concentrated internal variance, motivating a regularizer that substantially reduces false refusals in experiments.

paragraphs: This paper studies optimization with Gaussian processes when an adversary can introduce unknown and potentially changing perturbations. Its objective is robust satisficing: repeatedly achieving a chosen performance threshold despite those disturbances. This changes the target from maximizing worst-case performance to reliably reaching a level considered sufficient.

The authors propose two algorithms based on different formulations of that objective and place both within a general framework. Their theoretical guarantees reflect different assumptions. One regret bound grows sublinearly with time when conditions on the adversary and the threshold hold. Another scales with the magnitude of the perturbations and requires no assumptions on the adversary.

Experiments show that the proposed approach achieves the satisficing objective more effectively than established robust optimization methods. The advantage is particularly evident when the comparison framework's ambiguity set, which describes the uncertainty it considers, is specified inaccurately. The findings make threshold selection central to the problem and show how different guarantees accommodate different levels of knowledge about adversarial behavior.
neurips-2025-robust-satisficing-gaussian.tldr: Two Gaussian-process algorithms target reliable threshold attainment under adversarial perturbations, with guarantees that depend on different assumptions about the adversary.

paragraphs: Neural networks can learn nonlinear system dynamics from observations, but accurate fits do not automatically provide physically plausible or stable forecasts. Purely data-driven models can struggle when extrapolating and may learn unstable behavior. This paper introduces an architecture that builds physical structure and stability into the learned dynamics.

Stable port-Hamiltonian neural networks incorporate biases based on energy conservation and dissipation while ensuring global Lyapunov stability. These constraints shape the kinds of dynamics the model can represent. The approach therefore uses physical knowledge as part of the learning architecture, connecting predictions to energy behavior and a mathematical stability property.

Illustrative and real-world examples show robust learning of stable dynamics from sparse data. The authors report better accuracy and more physically meaningful generalization than purely data-driven approaches, while avoiding instability. They also demonstrate applicability on multi-physics simulation data for surrogate modeling. The results support the usefulness of strong physical biases when the learning objective includes stability and plausible behavior beyond the available observations.
neurips-2025-stable-port-hamiltonian-neu.tldr: Stable port-Hamiltonian neural networks embed energy conservation, dissipation, and global stability into models that learn dynamics from sparse data.

paragraphs: Operator eigenvalue problems arise across science and engineering, but conventional numerical methods can become expensive in high dimensions. Neural approaches offer an alternative, although their accuracy depends strongly on how eigenvalues are distributed. STNet uses that dependence constructively by transforming the operator during learning to make the desired solutions easier to find.

At each iteration, approximate eigenvalues and eigenfunctions guide a transformation into an equivalent, more manageable problem. One component, deflation projection, removes the subspace associated with eigenfunctions already found. This reduces the search space and helps prevent repeated convergence to existing solutions. A second component filters the spectrum, amplifying eigenvalues in the target region while suppressing those outside it.

These transformations respond to the paper's observation that larger spectral gaps improve the precision of learning-based methods. Experiments show that STNet consistently exceeds the accuracy of existing learning-based approaches and achieves state-of-the-art results in the reported comparisons. The contribution is an iterative strategy that uses partial solutions to reshape the remaining search problem.
neurips-2025-stnet-spectral-transformati.tldr: STNet improves neural eigenvalue solving by excluding known solutions and transforming the spectrum to emphasize the eigenvalues being sought.

paragraphs: People often switch languages within a conversation or even a single utterance. Speech recognition systems designed around one language can struggle with this behavior, while existing code-switching datasets often cover only two languages within relatively homogeneous speaker groups. SwitchLingua expands the linguistic and speaker diversity available for studying this challenge.

The authors introduce LinguaMaster, a multi-agent framework for scalable multilingual text synthesis, and use it to curate 420,000 code-switching text samples across 12 languages. The accompanying audio contains more than 80 hours recorded by 174 speakers representing 18 countries or regions and 63 racial or ethnic backgrounds. This combines synthesized text with recordings based on that text.

The paper also proposes Semantic-Aware Error Rate, which incorporates meaning into evaluation to better reflect code-switching performance. Benchmarking state-of-the-art speech recognition models reveals substantial performance gaps on SwitchLingua. These results establish the dataset as a demanding evaluation resource, while its broader coverage supports research on multilingual speech technology across diverse linguistic and cultural contexts.
neurips-2025-switchlingua-the-first-larg.tldr: SwitchLingua provides diverse multilingual code-switching text and speech, alongside a meaning-aware metric that exposes gaps in current speech recognition.

paragraphs: Gaussian sketching transforms data by multiplying it by a random Gaussian matrix. Besides its computational benefits, the randomness can provide differential privacy guarantees. This paper revisits the privacy analysis of that operation, asking how tightly its privacy properties can be characterized using Rényi differential privacy.

The main contribution is a refined analysis that gives significantly tighter privacy bounds than previous results. Those bounds provide a sharper account of the protection supplied by the random transformation. The authors then use the improved analysis in several linear regression settings and establish theoretical guarantees for the resulting utility. This links the privacy calculation to the quality of the statistical task performed on the transformed data.

Experiments across multiple datasets report improved performance, with runtime reductions in several cases. The stated gains therefore extend beyond a tighter mathematical bound: the revised analysis supports better regression methods in the evaluated settings. Runtime improvements are reported for some cases, while performance improvements span multiple datasets.
neurips-2025-the-gaussian-mixing-mechani.tldr: A tighter Rényi differential privacy analysis of Gaussian sketching yields improved linear regression utility and, in several cases, lower runtime.

paragraphs: Image watermarking supports authenticity and attribution, but security evaluation often concentrates on removing marks. This paper examines forging: transferring a watermark from genuine content to other content. That threat matters because a watermark can be misleading even when it remains detectable, if its presence no longer reliably indicates the claimed origin.

The authors introduce an image preference model that estimates whether an image is watermarked. It is trained with a ranking loss using procedurally generated images, without requiring real watermarks for training. They then demonstrate watermark removal and forgery through image optimization guided by the model. The attack uses a single watermarked reference image and does not require knowledge of the watermarking model.

Evaluation spans multiple post-hoc image watermarking models and demonstrates effective forgery. These findings identify an attribution weakness in the tested approaches and broaden the security question beyond resistance to removal. The contribution is especially relevant to practical evaluation because the demonstrated attack needs limited access: one marked image and no internal knowledge of the target watermarking system.
neurips-2025-transferable-black-box-one-.tldr: A preference model trained without real watermarks enables black-box watermark forgery from one marked image across multiple tested watermarking systems.

paragraphs: Three-dimensional Gaussian diffusion models can be slow because generation processes many Gaussian primitives through repeated denoising and subsequent processing. Considering multiple sampling trajectories adds further cost. TRIM is a post-training approach that reduces work along both the trajectory dimension and the spatial content of each candidate.

For trajectory reduction, a lightweight selector evaluates latent Gaussian primitives produced from multiple noise samples. It identifies candidates with promising quality early, reducing the need to carry every trajectory through an expensive complete generation process. For spatial reduction, instance mask denoising filters redundant background regions and prunes Gaussian primitives, lowering computation at each denoising step.

The two strategies target complementary sources of expense: how many candidates receive continued processing and how much content each step processes. Experiments and analysis report significant improvements in both generation efficiency and quality. The findings support scaling inference by evaluating multiple candidates while selectively allocating further computation, with the proposed pruning also reducing the cost of the trajectories that continue.
neurips-2025-trim-scalable-3d-gaussian-d.tldr: TRIM accelerates three-dimensional Gaussian diffusion by selecting promising trajectories early and pruning redundant background primitives during denoising.

paragraphs: A regression model's prediction does not fully describe which outcomes are plausible. Prediction intervals add a range, but can still hide important features such as asymmetry or multiple likely outcomes. This paper addresses the need for richer uncertainty information without requiring changes to, or retraining of, an already trained predictive model.

MCNF is a post hoc uncertainty method based on contextualised normalizing flows. It operates on top of the existing predictor and produces both prediction intervals and a full conditioned predictive distribution. Providing the distribution preserves information that an interval alone leaves out, giving downstream decisions access to the shape of the estimated uncertainty.

Experiments provide evidence that MCNF's uncertainty estimates are well calibrated and competitive with state-of-the-art uncertainty quantification methods. The authors also report that the richer output helps inform downstream decision-making tasks. Its practical contribution is the combination of distribution-level information with compatibility with an existing trained predictor, avoiding the predictive-model retraining required by the Bayesian approaches discussed in the paper.
neurips-2025-uncertainty-quantification-.tldr: MCNF adds calibrated prediction intervals and full conditional uncertainty distributions to trained regression models without retraining the predictor.

paragraphs: Vision-language models can struggle to plan actions in unfamiliar environments, especially when goals require many steps. The paper attributes part of this difficulty to imitation learning that separates instructions from environmental context. Models may consequently rely on supplementary cues and have trouble interpreting instructions whose meaning depends on what they observe.

World-Aware Planning Narrative Enhancement, or WAP, develops environmental understanding through four capabilities: modeling visual appearance, spatial reasoning, functional abstraction, and syntactic grounding. It uses curriculum learning and develops and evaluates models using only raw visual observations. The approach connects planning instructions to the environment through a structured set of capabilities for understanding what is visible and how it relates to a task.

On EB-ALFRED, the authors report a 60.7 absolute improvement in Qwen2.5-VL's task success rates, with gains of 60.0 for commonsense reasoning and 70.0 for long-horizon planning. Enhanced open-source models also outperform GPT-4o and Claude-3.5-Sonnet by a large margin in this evaluation. These findings support grounding planning training more closely in environmental understanding.
neurips-2025-world-aware-planning-narrat.tldr: WAP strengthens vision-language planning through curriculum-based environmental understanding, producing substantial gains on the EB-ALFRED benchmark.
